new_statements.translation: Nadêb is a fixed-stress language, with stress always falling on the last syllable of the word, as can be seen in the examples in (100): /ta'wog/ 'his belly', /ba'ho:d/ 'wind'. ... It was established that Nadêb is a fixed-stress language, with stress always falling on the last syllable of the word, and that stress is responsible for the phonological process of vowel-length reduction when a long vowel stands in a pretonic syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the word; non-contrastive. Long vowels do not surface (are shortened) in open pretonic syllables, and only reduced vowel allophones [ɪ ə ʊ] occur there. The language has no tone; vowel length and laryngealization are the contrastive suprasegmentals. Independently confirmed for the Roçado and Rio Negro dialects by Martins 2005 (LOT 104), sec. 2.2.4 p. 69: 'Os dialetos Nadëb têm um sistema acentual fixo na última sílaba' and 2.2.5 'Os dialetos Nadëb não possuem tons'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in Barbosa 2005 or Martins 2005.
new_statements.exceptions: Proclitic (non-independent) personal pronouns are phonologically bound and unstressed (Barbosa p. 54; Weir 1984). Weir 1984 notes most verbal suffixes are monosyllabic and unstressed while the suffix manɨh is stressed on its second syllable, and incorporated elements keep their own stress -- i.e. the stress domain is the phonological word/root plus stress-bearing suffixes; no lexical exceptions to final stress are reported.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('última sílaba da palavra'), illustrated with citation forms including possessor-proclitic + noun (/ta'wog/ 'his belly') where the proclitic is unstressed and stress is final. Barbosa's data are from the Paraná Boá-Boá (Jutaí community) variety; Martins 2005 gives the same rule for the Roçado and Rio Negro dialects.
new_statements.identity_note: Barbosa 2005 describes the Nadëb variety of the Paraná Boá-Boá Indigenous Territory (Jutaí community, Japurá basin); Martins 2005 covers the Roçado (upper Uneiuxi) and Rio Negro (Bom Jardim, 'Kuyawí') dialects and states the same fixed: final syllable rule for both, so the statement holds for Nadëb (nade1244) as a whole. Glottolog lists no separate dialect codes that need distinguishing here.

new_statements.translation: Nadêb is a fixed-stress language, in which stress always falls on the last syllable of the word, as can be seen in the examples in (100). (100) /ta 'wog/ 'his belly' /ba 'ho:d/ 'wind' [p. 49] ... It was found that Nadêb is a fixed-stress language, in which stress always falls on the last syllable of the word, and that stress is responsible for the phonological process characterized by reduction of vowel duration, if the vowel is long and is in a pretonic syllable. [p. 57] ... The Nadëb dialects do not have tones. Duration and laryngealization perform the function formerly held by the tone that existed in Proto Eastern Makú. (Martins 2005:70) [quoted p. 53]

new_statements.relation_note: Same work as the existing statement (the MPG '2008' record is the 2005 UnB dissertation: dateAccepted 2005, datePublishedInPrint 2008, and its public file link points to the etnolinguistica.org copy already held by the project). Fixed final stress = catalog final stress. Adds: no tone (via Martins 2005), and the pretonic shortening effect. The MPG landing page itself could not be opened (Anubis proof-of-work 403 on both the handle redirect and pure.mpg.de); the REST metadata was downloaded on the second attempt and shows the MPG-hosted PDF is audience-restricted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of every word; no tone; long vowels and laryngealization do not occur in open pretonic syllables (long vowels shorten there), so stress conditions the distribution of the length/laryngealization contrasts.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated ('sempre' / always). One incidental remark (p. 26, summarizing Weir) that postpositions incorporated into the verb lose their own stress when they become prefixes; the corpus is a c. 800-word list plus short sentences from Paraná Boá-Boá.
new_statements.identity_note: Barbosa's data are from the Paraná Boá-Boá (Japurá) dialect of Nadêb; he states (p. 57-58) that it shares the characteristics of the Roçado dialect described by Senn & Senn 1998, apart from some segmental differences. Martins 2005 covers the Roçado and Rio Negro (Kuyawí) dialects with the same final-stress finding, so the fixed: final syllable reading holds across the described dialects.
